## Chapter 44: Intermediate Graphical Analysis

### Additional Graphical Analysis Tools

As with many other areas of Six Sigma methodology, it's easy to overdo it when it comes to graphical analysis — particularly when presenting information to other people. With so many tools available, it's tempting to pick the chart that's new, interesting, or most complex. Often, though, that means spending non-value-added time creating a visual tool when a simpler tool would solve the problem. If you remember Chapter 18, that would be a case of overprocessing to avoid.

Consider the two charts below to understand when overprocessing might be occurring with respect to graphical analysis.

<img alt="Gráfico de barras simples: Erros de Vendas por vendedor (A a G)" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:475px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

<img alt="O mesmo dado como gráfico de Pareto: Erros de Vendas com linha de porcentagem acumulada" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:473px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


Both charts are a graphical representation of the same information. The first is a simple bar chart, created with a few clicks in Excel. The second is a Pareto chart, also created in Excel, but requiring many more mouse clicks. In this particular case, a Pareto chart isn't necessary to convey the required information. The data is distinct enough that anyone can see, just by looking at the bar chart, that salesperson E is responsible for a large share of the errors. In this particular case, the Pareto chart is over-engineering the conclusion and doesn't need to be created if it requires extra work.

In this example, it's possible that a visual representation of the data isn't even necessary: the conclusion is obvious. Looking at the raw data below, you quickly notice that employee E has three times as many errors as the employee with the next-most errors. Even when raw data allows for easy analysis, however, many Six Sigma practitioners still take the time to create a graphical representation for presentation purposes. A chart is visually more appealing and faster to read than a data table.

The simplest graphical analysis isn't always the best choice, especially when the data elements aren't as obvious. A more complex analysis may be needed to uncover outliers, relationships, and trends. Even when conclusions about the data seem obvious, they aren't always correct. This is especially true when dealing with the relationship or correlation between factors in a process.

As a Six Sigma practitioner, it takes time to be able to quickly choose which type of graphical analysis will best represent the data at hand. It's also important to note that the best choice for graphical analysis depends both on the questions being asked and on the data itself. In the example above, the basic bar chart is a good choice for a team that wants to know where the errors might be coming from. If the team were comparing errors against shift hours worked, the bar chart wouldn't be useful.

While it's true that you don't want to waste time and space presenting data in a way that doesn't help — or that could be considered overproduction muda — the same isn't always true when it comes to analysis. During the analyze phase of a DMAIC project, Black Belts and other Six Sigma practitioners frequently work with numerous graphical analysis tools while trying to understand the data. The need to visualize data in multiple ways is one of the reasons statistical analysis software is useful: such software removes some of the manual work of creating these charts. Trial-and-error work with every type of Six Sigma analysis tool also helps you learn to identify which tools best fit each situation.

In this section, we'll discuss a few tools not yet presented, covering benefits, limitations, and how to build the tools in Excel without statistical analysis software, when needed.

### Bar Charts

One of the biggest benefits of bar charts is that they're recognizable and easy to read. Practically any employee at a company can pull information from a well-formatted bar chart without instruction or guidance, making them a great choice for general-purpose presentations and training materials. Bar charts are also easy to create, so they're a preferred method of illustration in presentations and reports.

Other benefits include:

- The ability to summarize large data sets in a simple visual format
- The ability to clarify trends
- The fact that most people can easily estimate important values on a well-formatted bar chart
- The ability to visually check the data and identify areas where the data might be skewed
- The ability to easily display data sets that vary above and below zero on the same chart

Bar charts typically require nominal or ordinal data — data classified according to qualitative information. When displaying nominal data, it's often beneficial to create a Pareto-style chart, so the reader instantly sees how the population relates to the categories. Ordinal data usually comes with its own logical order of presentation. For example, if individuals are asked to rate satisfaction with a product as very satisfied, somewhat satisfied, neutral, dissatisfied, and very dissatisfied, then you generally wouldn't want to change the order of that presentation in a bar chart.

Bar charts aren't free of limitations. Depending on what's being presented, additional narrative may be needed to explain the chart. Bar charts also often fail to reveal key information about trends that aren't part of the chart's specific design, and rarely, on their own, provide detailed data about causes or patterns in the data. Finally, it's easy to manipulate the colors, order, and layout of a bar chart to influence the message the audience takes away. Six Sigma practitioners should always choose the best format to display underlying truths, but should never format a chart to create an impression that might not match the statistical data behind the graphical representation.

Most versions of Excel offer several types of bar charts, and you can experiment with these various formats to see how they display your data. Some observations on common formats are included below.

**Column vs. Bar**

Technically, what's commonly called a "bar chart" — and what we've been calling a bar chart here — is a column chart. The visual columns representing each data category rise vertically. A literal bar chart displays the same information horizontally. Most versions of Excel let you choose between the two displays. The information from the sample data table is shown below in a horizontal bar chart.

<img alt="Gráfico de barras horizontal: chamadas telefônicas por hora" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:588px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


**3D Bar and Column Charts**

The charts shown so far in this chapter are all two-dimensional. Excel can also help you create three-dimensional charts, to add visual appeal to a presentation. 3D charts are useful if you're presenting several similar-looking charts in sequence, since they help differentiate the information in your presentation. It can also be useful to create more visually appealing charts simply to more fully capture the audience's attention. Here's an example of the same data used above, in a 3D chart.

<img alt="Gráfico de colunas 3D: chamadas telefônicas por hora" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:467px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


**Stacked Bar Charts**

Stacked bar charts let you display the total of nominal or ordinal data for each category, while simultaneously breaking that information down into color-coded categories. For example, if the Six Sigma team analyzing calls by hour wanted to display data that included how many calls were handled by separate teams within a department, the bar chart might look like the image below.

#### Creating a Stacked Bar Chart

To create a stacked bar chart, you need nominal or ordinal data split into categories. The categories need to be the same for each data set, so that the total of the subcategory numbers equals the total of the main category. For example, if you have three bags of marbles, you might have data that says:

<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Bag</th>
<th>Number of marbles</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>1</td>
<td>10</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>2</td>
<td>3</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>3</td>
<td>15</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

After further analysis, you notice that you have marbles in three colors: red, blue, and yellow.

<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th></th>
<th>Bag 1</th>
<th>Bag 2</th>
<th>Bag 3</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Red</td>
<td>7</td>
<td>1</td>
<td>5</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Yellow</td>
<td>3</td>
<td>1</td>
<td>8</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Blue</td>
<td>0</td>
<td>1</td>
<td>2</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

Bag 1 doesn't include any blue marbles, but you still need to include blue as a category for Bag 1, because it's a category in the other two bags. You simply put a 0 in that data field. Note that each bag's subcategory totals add up to the number of marbles in that bag. Following these guidelines — including every subcategory for each section and making sure the subcategories add up correctly — helps you build accurate stacked bar charts.

#### Worked example on five fronts: Bar and Pie Chart

Revisiting the **Sales Errors by Employee** table from the text above: A=10, B=5, C=2, D=9, E=34, F=7, G=3.

<img alt="Ilustracao Excel + Power BI (DAX) do exemplo: Gráfico de Barras e de Pizza" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," style="max-width:100%;" />

**Excel 365**: highlight the two columns → **Insert → Chart → Bar Chart** (columns) or **Insert → Chart → Pie Chart** for the proportional version.

**Power BI (DAX)** — a proportion measure over a table `ErrosVendas[Funcionario, Erros]`, used for both the bar chart and the pie chart:

```dax
% do Total = DIVIDE ( SUM ( ErrosVendas[Erros] ), CALCULATE ( SUM ( ErrosVendas[Erros] ), ALL ( ErrosVendas ) ) )
```

```py-r
--- python
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Funcionário": ["A","B","C","D","E","F","G"],
    "Erros": [10, 5, 2, 9, 34, 7, 3],
})
df["% do Total"] = df["Erros"] / df["Erros"].sum() * 100
print(df.round(1).to_string(index=False))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4))
axes[0].bar(df["Funcionário"], df["Erros"], color="#00688f")
axes[0].set_title("Gráfico de barras")
# 7 fatias excedem qualquer paleta categórica. Como as fatias já estão
# rotuladas, a cor não carrega identidade: usa-se uma rampa de UMA cor,
# ordenada por magnitude — e não sete matizes inventados.
rampa = ["#0d3d4f", "#0f5169", "#00688f", "#3d8dab", "#6fa8be", "#a3c8d5", "#d6e7ee"]
ordem = df["Erros"].rank(ascending=False).astype(int) - 1
axes[1].pie(df["Erros"], labels=df["Funcionário"], autopct="%1.0f%%",
            colors=[rampa[k] for k in ordem])
axes[1].set_title("Gráfico de pizza")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```py-r
--- python
%%R
funcionario <- c("A","B","C","D","E","F","G")
erros <- c(10, 5, 2, 9, 34, 7, 3)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
barplot(erros, names.arg = funcionario, col = "#00688f", main = "Barras")
pie(erros, labels = funcionario, main = "Pizza")

cat("% do total (E):", round(erros[5] / sum(erros) * 100, 1), "\n")
```

**Minitab** (current version — check minitab.com): paste Employee into C1 and Errors into C2, then **Graph → Bar Chart** (or **Graph → Pie Chart**), with *Categorical variable* = C1 and *Values from a table* = C2.

*Cross-check note: all five methods agree that employee E accounts for 34/70 ≈ 48.6% of the errors — more than three times the runner-up (D, 9) — confirming the text's point that a Pareto chart would be overprocessing here: the conclusion is already obvious in a simple bar chart.*

### Pie Charts

The pie chart is another visual tool that practically any employee in a business setting will be familiar with, making it a good choice for displaying certain types of information. Ordinal and nominal information can also be displayed in a pie chart, with the main purpose of visually representing how each category relates to the whole. Conventional wisdom says to use a pie chart when the numbers you're representing add up to 100, but that doesn't have to be the case. Excel converts values into percentages to build pie charts. Consider the pie chart below, representing the numbers 8, 5, and 4. Excel considers each of these numbers relative to the total of the "pie," which is 17. The blue slice, representing 47%, corresponds to the raw figure 8/17.

<img alt="Gráfico de pizza simples com fatias representando os valores 8, 5 e 4" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:497px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


The benefits of pie charts include:

- The ability to summarize large amounts of specific types of data in a visual format.
- Simplicity; the pie chart is one of the simplest chart types.
- The ability to identify obvious problems with the data or calculations.
- Pie charts usually require very little additional explanation, when labeled correctly.
- Pie charts display the relevance of subset data within a total data set.

The fact that pie charts are constantly used in business settings is both an advantage and a disadvantage for Six Sigma teams and practitioners. When data can be represented in a pie chart, the Six Sigma practitioner generally needs less narrative to convey a potential point. At the same time, pie charts don't always carry the same weight that a more advanced statistical representation might, because business employees are so used to seeing them. Other disadvantages of pie charts include the fact that they can be manipulated in much the same way as bar charts, they often fail to easily display changes over time, and it can be hard to visualize exact values when presented in a pie chart.

<img alt="Gráfico de pizza resultante: minutos por etapa do processo (A a J)" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:523px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


From the pie chart built for our sample data, we can see that roughly half of the total process time relates to just two steps out of the 10-step process. We can also quickly see which steps take the longest, on average, and which are the shortest, although we can't draw conclusions about the actual time from this chart alone.

As with bar charts, you can take advantage of Excel's options to create three-dimensional pie charts. A particularly useful feature is Excel's Pie of Pie function, which lets you build an overall pie chart and pull out a second pie chart to zoom in on certain areas of the larger structure. Consider the Pie of Pie chart below, which represents the same data as the pie chart above.

<img alt="Gráfico Pizza de Pizza: a pizza principal com um pedaço destacado em uma pizza secundária menor, dividindo-o em quatro subcategorias (A a J)" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:633px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


The original pie chart represented 10 steps. The illustration above shows a large pie chart with a secondary chart. The large pie chart appears to show 7 steps — but that pie chart shows the same information as the one above. However, four process steps are pulled out into a smaller chart, so you can see how they relate to each other more clearly. Those four steps combined form the seventh, dark-blue slice of the larger pie. This makes it easier to identify the relevance of smaller data categories within the whole, or to emphasize a particular area of the chart.

You do need to be careful, though, that whoever is viewing it doesn't attribute relevance or importance based solely on the size of the pie slices. The gray slice in the secondary chart above is larger than some of the other slices in the larger pie, but that doesn't mean that step takes longer. The smaller pie should be thought of as a zoomed-in view of one small slice of the overall chart. In this case, that small slice accounts for four of the steps.

### XY Scatter Diagrams

We introduced scatter diagrams very briefly in Chapter 36, and we'll revisit them in depth in later chapters on correlation and regression modeling. In this section, we'll cover how to create a scatter diagram in Excel, without any analysis add-in. In Chapter 46, we'll use an Excel add-in to run some statistical analysis while creating scatter diagrams.

Scatter diagrams are beneficial because they can help teams visually see the relationship between two factors in a process. Does temperature decrease over time? Does a person's productivity increase with their pay? These are examples of questions that scatter diagrams can answer, but it's important to realize that correlation, as represented in a scatter diagram, doesn't necessarily mean causation. Two variables can be closely related without one causing changes in the other.

Scatter diagrams typically help teams see whether there's no correlation, weak correlation, or positive or negative correlation. Positive correlation occurs when variable 2 is related to an increase in variable 1, or vice versa. Negative correlation occurs when variable 2 is related to a decrease in variable 1, or vice versa. For example, it's commonly observed that crime rate and average per-capita income in geographic areas across the United States are related. Areas showing higher crime rates often also show lower income statistics. The statement can be made in the other direction: areas showing lower income statistics often show higher crime rates. That's not to say that either of these things necessarily causes the other.

The downsides of scatter diagrams are that they aren't as familiar to business employees as bar charts, pie charts, or even line charts. There's also the risk that individuals without an understanding of statistical analysis will confuse correlation with causation, which can lead to incorrect decisions. Black Belts and other Six Sigma practitioners need to be aware of these risks, so they can properly explain scatter diagrams and provide additional explanation when needed.

From the scatter diagram built here, we can see that the two variables — production volume and errors — appear to be related in some way. While it's a good bet that increasing production actually causes an increase in errors, you can't simply assume causation from this chart. That assumption could be tested further using more advanced statistical techniques.

It's worth noting that, even when correlation seems obvious in a scatter diagram, that isn't always the case. Six Sigma practitioners should always test correlation assumptions, to make sure they're statistically correct, before presenting a scatter diagram to others as an illustration of a relationship. We'll cover statistical tests of regression and correlation in Chapter 46.

#### Worked example on five fronts: Scatter Diagram

Revisiting the **Parts per Hour vs. Defects** table from the text above (9 points). The formal statistical test of correlation (not just the coefficient) is covered in detail in Chapter 46 — here the focus is on building the diagram and the descriptive coefficient.

<img alt="Ilustracao Excel + Power BI (DAX) do exemplo: Diagrama de Dispersão" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," style="max-width:100%;" />

**Excel 365**: highlight the two columns (Parts Per Hour, Defects) → **Insert → Chart → Scatter**. The correlation coefficient uses `=CORREL(A2:A10,B2:B10)`.

**Power BI (DAX)** — a correlation (Pearson) measure via a direct summation formula, over a table `Producao[Pecas, Defeitos]`:

```dax
Correlacao Pecas Defeitos =
VAR N = COUNTROWS ( Producao )
VAR SomaXY = SUMX ( Producao, Producao[Pecas] * Producao[Defeitos] )
VAR SomaX = SUM ( Producao[Pecas] )
VAR SomaY = SUM ( Producao[Defeitos] )
VAR SomaX2 = SUMX ( Producao, Producao[Pecas] ^ 2 )
VAR SomaY2 = SUMX ( Producao, Producao[Defeitos] ^ 2 )
RETURN
    DIVIDE (
        N * SomaXY - SomaX * SomaY,
        SQRT ( ( N * SomaX2 - SomaX ^ 2 ) * ( N * SomaY2 - SomaY ^ 2 ) )
    )
```

Pearson correlation is a direct (closed-form) calculation, so DAX solves it natively — this isn't a "visualization only" case.

```py-r
--- python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

pecas = [100, 150, 200, 250, 300, 350, 400, 450, 500]
defeitos = [3, 4, 5, 5, 7, 7, 9, 8, 10]

corr = np.corrcoef(pecas, defeitos)[0, 1]
print(f"Coeficiente de correlação: {corr:.4f}")

plt.figure(figsize=(5, 4))
plt.scatter(pecas, defeitos, color="#00688f")
plt.xlabel("Peças por hora")
plt.ylabel("Defeitos")
plt.title("Diagrama de dispersão")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```py-r
--- python
%%R
pecas <- c(100, 150, 200, 250, 300, 350, 400, 450, 500)
defeitos <- c(3, 4, 5, 5, 7, 7, 9, 8, 10)

cat("Coeficiente de correlacao:", round(cor(pecas, defeitos), 4), "\n")
plot(pecas, defeitos, pch = 16, col = "#00688f",
     xlab = "Pecas por hora", ylab = "Defeitos", main = "Diagrama de dispersao")
```

**Minitab** (current version — check minitab.com): paste Parts into C1 and Defects into C2, then **Graph → Scatterplot → Simple**.

*Cross-check note: all five methods agree on a correlation coefficient of ≈ 0.971 — a strong positive correlation between production volume and defects, confirming the text's visual reading (without, yet, proving causation — that's the subject of Chapter 46).*

### Creating an X-bar Control Chart in Excel 365

The X-bar control chart plots a sample's mean over time — or the mean of samples collected over time, in the case of an active process. X-bar control charts are among the most frequently used control charts. Minitab (Unit 5) remains the fastest option, with instability tests already built in, but Excel 365 can build a functional control chart with reference lines that update themselves, using the same helper-column-with-absolute-reference trick as the run chart (Unit 3).

1. Enter your data points in column A.
2. In two separate cells, calculate the mean with `=AVERAGE(A2:A15)` and the sample standard deviation with `=STDEV.S(A2:A15)`.
3. From those two values, calculate the control limits: UCL = Mean + 3×StdDev; LCL = Mean − 3×StdDev.
4. Create a helper column for each reference line (UCL, Mean, LCL), repeating the constant value on every row with an absolute reference — for example, `=$G$2` for UCL down the entire column B.
5. Select the data columns and the reference columns, and choose **Insert → Charts → Insert Line or Area Chart → Line**.

(Practice with the following data.) **X-bar Data Points:** 24.1, 25.2, 24.7, 28.3, 27.1, 26.4, 25.4, 21.4, 24.5, 23.5, 27.5, 29.5, 24.5, 26.8

Excel plots all the series on the same chart: the varying data points, and each reference line perfectly straight and always up to date, because it comes from a formula with an absolute reference — unlike older versions of this technique, which required manually adjusting the Y-axis limits and applying formatting tricks (gradient line, marker removal) to keep the background lines discreet. In Excel 365, you just click each reference series and adjust thickness, color, or dash style from the formatting pane.

To add the ±1 and ±2 standard-deviation zones (used by the Unit 16 instability tests), repeat the same pattern: four more helper columns — Mean+1σ, Mean+2σ, Mean−1σ, Mean−2σ — each with an absolute reference, plotted as additional series on the same chart.

This process takes just a few minutes once you're familiar with the elements of a control chart, and it's worth knowing because Six Sigma practitioners don't always have immediate access to dedicated statistical software.

#### Worked example on five fronts: X-bar Control Chart

Using the **X-bar Data Points** from the exercise above (14 values). This example focuses on **building** the chart and its limits; automatic reading of the 8 special-cause tests on a series is in Chapter 38, and Chapter 67 (PART V) goes deeper into X-bar & R with subgroups.

<img alt="Ilustracao Excel + Power BI (DAX) do exemplo: Gráfico de Controle X-barra" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," style="max-width:100%;" />

**Excel 365**: steps already described above (mean, sample standard deviation, UCL/LCL with absolute-reference helper columns, then **Insert → Charts → Line**).

**Power BI (DAX)** — center line and limit measures, to plot alongside the series in the line chart, over a table `Processo[Ponto, Valor]`:

```dax
Linha Central = AVERAGE ( Processo[Valor] )
Desvio Padrao = STDEV.S ( Processo[Valor] )
UCL = [Linha Central] + 3 * [Desvio Padrao]
LCL = [Linha Central] - 3 * [Desvio Padrao]
```

Same case as Chapter 8: mean, standard deviation, and simple limits are native DAX calculations.

```py-r
--- python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

dados = [24.1,25.2,24.7,28.3,27.1,26.4,25.4,21.4,24.5,23.5,27.5,29.5,24.5,26.8]

linha_central = np.mean(dados)
sigma = np.std(dados, ddof=1)
ucl, lcl = linha_central + 3*sigma, linha_central - 3*sigma

print(f"Linha central: {linha_central:.3f}")
print(f"Desvio padrão amostral: {sigma:.3f}")
print(f"UCL: {ucl:.3f}   LCL: {lcl:.3f}")

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))
plt.plot(range(1, 15), dados, marker="o", color="#00688f", label="Pontos")
plt.axhline(linha_central, color="#16232a", label="Linha central")
plt.axhline(ucl, color="#5f93a5", linestyle="--", label="UCL")
plt.axhline(lcl, color="#5f93a5", linestyle="--", label="LCL")
plt.title("Gráfico de Controle X-barra")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```py-r
--- python
%%R
dados <- c(24.1,25.2,24.7,28.3,27.1,26.4,25.4,21.4,24.5,23.5,27.5,29.5,24.5,26.8)

linha_central <- mean(dados)
sigma <- sd(dados)
ucl <- linha_central + 3*sigma
lcl <- linha_central - 3*sigma
cat(sprintf("Linha central: %.3f\n", linha_central))
cat(sprintf("Desvio padrao amostral: %.3f\n", sigma))
cat(sprintf("UCL: %.3f   LCL: %.3f\n", ucl, lcl))

plot(1:14, dados, type = "o", pch = 16, col = "#00688f",
     xlab = "Ponto", ylab = "Valor", main = "Grafico de Controle X-barra",
     ylim = c(lcl - 1, ucl + 1))
abline(h = linha_central, col = "#16232a")
abline(h = c(ucl, lcl), col = "#5f93a5", lty = 2)
```

**Minitab** (current version — check minitab.com): paste the 14 values into C1 and go to **Stat → Control Charts → Variables Charts for Individuals → Individuals**. Minitab calculates the center line and limits automatically and already applies the Chapter 38 special-cause tests on the same screen.

*Cross-check note: all five methods converge on a center line ≈ 25.636, UCL ≈ 31.981, LCL ≈ 19.291 — Python and R match exactly. Excel and DAX are checked manually against these numbers; no point exceeds the limits in this series.*

### Enabling the Analysis ToolPak in Excel 365

You can do these calculations manually, which helps you understand the reasoning behind an analysis, but we'll also rely heavily on the Analysis ToolPak — Microsoft's free statistical add-in, included in all current versions of Excel, including Excel for the Web within Microsoft 365. It doesn't come enabled by default.

1. Go to **File → Options → Add-ins**.
2. Find the Analysis ToolPak in the list of inactive add-ins. If it's already in the list of active add-ins, skip to step 5 — it's already ready to use.
3. In the **Manage** box at the bottom, confirm "Excel Add-ins" is selected and click **Go**.
4. Check the Analysis ToolPak box and click **OK**. (The "Analysis ToolPak – VBA" item is a different add-in; it isn't needed for statistical analysis.)
5. Confirm activation by opening the **Data** tab on the ribbon: the **Data Analysis** button appears in the rightmost group.
